subject: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model

messages.author: 552cec1104f5ec25
messages.subject: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
parts:
Dear all,


I’m trying to understand a very simple multi-logit regression, but my intuition is not matching up to the results I am getting….. perhaps I am missing something fundamental.



In the attached R file I generate data from a categorical distribution in which there are 6 equally probably outcomes.


I then fit the model using a simplified version of the multi_logit model from the stan user manual (see attached multi_logit.stan). Once fitted I then transform the beta parameter to a vector of probabilities using the softmax function.


When I fit the model with reasonably large N then the theta parameters recover the true value (1/6) well.


However, if I fit the model with very few data points (say N = 2) the 90% intervals are often quite narrow and exclude the 1/6 value. For example, the attached plot shows the intervals I generated with N = 2. My intuition is that these intervals should span 1/6 with a high degree of uncertainty (i.e. be very wide)…



My question is – why is this not the case? 



Many thanks,


Oscar

messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
parts:
Howdy Oscar!

Your question is perfectly reasonable, but I think you'll have a better time working directly with the theta simplex and a Dirichlet prior. I attached a modified model.

The Dirichlet distribution is the conjugate prior for the categorical, so there are analytical solutions for this model (the posterior is also a Dirichlet distribution -- here's a pretty terse version of that): https://people.eecs.berkeley.edu/~stephentu/writeups/dirichlet-conjugate-prior.pdf

The neat thing about the Dirichlet prior is that the parameters correspond pretty closely (they're real numbers > 0, so not exactly...) to how many times you've seen each object before, and because it's conjugate we can get the posterior by simply updating these parameters with how many more samples we see.

The prior (pcounts) specified in the model says we've seen each object once. Mess around with this prior and see how your posterior estimates change and see if this makes more sense to you.

Ben

messages.author: 552cec1104f5ec25
messages.subject: Re: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
parts:
Hi Ben,

Thanks for taking a look for me! I very much appreciate it. 

Your model makes a lot of sense! And much more intuitive. I guess that while this solution is great for the problem I've posted, it's not so easy when you want to expand the model to have multiple predictors? 

I see now that I really hadn't thought through the implications of the normal prior on beta. When the scale parameter of the prior is 5 (as in the model) it's placing quite a strong prior on theta values being near zero, with a smaller peak near 1. So the over fitting makes sense to me now. 

And when the scale parameter of the normal prior gets smaller the more the density shifts to equal probabilities across outcomes. So I can probably aim for something sensible and then fit the models with a few different priors. 

I wonder what the least informative prior would be for 6 outcomes? 

All the best,

Oscar

messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: Understanding a very simple multi-logit model
parts:
"Least informative" could mean a few different things I think. From the BDA3 book, page 69, the Dirichlet prior with all the alphas equal to 1 samples uniformly from all K-simplexes, so that means you're not favoring any set of probabilities over another one (the x dependence goes away in the pdf if all alphas == 1, make plots of the pdf of a 3-value Dirichlet distribution with various parameters to convince yourself of this).

I don't think it's a crime to put hyperpriors on your Dirichlet distribution either if that's the thing you aren't sure about. Google around for "multinomial dirichlet hyperprior" and you'll see folks talking about various things they've tried.

For the multiple predictors, you're moving into GLM territory I think. That's chapter 16 in BDA3, or check out the Rstanarm examples (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/pooling.html).

Ben

> On Apr 28, 2017, at 12:02 PM, Oscar <oscart...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Ben,
>
> Thanks for taking a look for me! I very much appreciate it.
>
> Your model makes a lot of sense! And much more intuitive. I guess that while this solution is great for the problem I've posted, it's not so easy when you want to expand the model to have multiple predictors?
>
> I see now that I really hadn't thought through the implications of the normal prior on beta. When the scale parameter of the prior is 5 (as in the model) it's placing quite a strong prior on theta values being near zero, with a smaller peak near 1. So the over fitting makes sense to me now.

It's not overfitting so much as model misspecification. If you
draw the parameters from the priors, then simulate data, you're
guaranteed to get proper coverage.

> And when the scale parameter of the normal prior gets smaller the more the density shifts to equal probabilities across outcomes. So I can probably aim for something sensible and then fit the models with a few different priors.
You should use whatever prior knowledge you actually have.
> I wonder what the least informative prior would be for 6 outcomes?

Ben Bales pointed out that the Dirichlet with unit vector is uniform.
That uniformity means you can just drop it from Stan if
you use a simplex. But that uniformity is with respect to a particular
parameterization. A prior that's uniform on one parameterization won't
be uniform on another, so you have to be careful about what you mean here.

For example, an improper uniform prior on log odds is nothing like
a uniform prior on the probabilities of getting an outcome.

- Bob

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Words of wisdom from Bob:  "It's not overfitting so much as model misspecification."
parts: I love this slogan of Bob's . . . maybe it could be embroidered and hung on the wall:
"It's not overfitting so much as model misspecification."

So true. If your model is correct, "overfitting" is impossible. In its usual form, "overfitting" comes from using too weak of a prior distribution.

A
